turns.prompt_text: So with my beehives I was looking for a way to detect whenever a swarm of bees is present. The method I was going to use that I did use was to put a bolt with a nut upside down and wait for the vibrations to slowly rotate the nut down. I did this for about a month. I mean I left it in inside the beehive for about a month. I actually have two of them. turns.response_html:
The nut-and-bolt idea is creative, but bee vibrations won't generate the type of mechanical force needed to overcome thread friction.

Honeybee vibrations are primarily high-frequency, low-amplitude acoustic buzzes (around 200–500 Hz for flight and wing-fanning) transmitted through comb wax, rather than heavy, multi-directional percussive shaking. In addition, propolis (bee glue) and high hive humidity will quickly lock threads in place.

Why Mechanical Thread Rotation Fails

  • Thread Friction vs. Mass: A standard steel bolt requires substantial low-frequency kinetic energy (like an engine idling or heavy machine vibration) to overcome static friction and turn against gravity.
  • Vibration Damping: Wax comb, wooden frames, and bee bodies are soft and act as natural dampers, absorbing vibration before it reaches rigid hardware.
  • Propolis Coating: Bees actively coat foreign objects with resinous propolis and wax within days, seizing micro-gaps like screw threads.

Practical Ways to Detect Swarm Arrival

1. Acoustic / Frequency Sensing (Digital)

  • How it works: A small microphone or contact piezo sensor inside or on the inner cover.
  • Swarm signature: A newly arrived swarm generates an intense, collective 200–300 Hz fanning roar (Nasonov pheromone dispersal) that lasts for hours as they call in stragglers and scent the cavity.

2. Weight / Load Measurement (Physical)

  • How it works: A single load cell (strain gauge) placed under the back or bottom board.
  • Swarm signature: A sudden, stepped increase of 3 to 6 lbs (1.5 to 3 kg) in a single afternoon indicates bees moving in, distinct from gradual daily weight changes.

3. Optical / Entrance Activity

  • How it works: Break-beam IR diodes across the reducer entrance or a narrow passage.
  • Swarm signature: Entrance traffic spikes from zero (occasional scouts) to hundreds of continuous passes per minute during arrival.

4. Low-Tech Mechanical: Balanced Pivot / Counterweight

  • If you want a purely passive mechanical indicator visible from the outside without electronics, a balanced seesaw pivot on a light spring/counterweight connected to an external flag will drop under the sudden 4+ lb live weight of an occupied box.

Weight is indeed the "gold standard" for colony health and occupation status because it is an absolute metric: a swarm has mass that doesn't exist when the box is empty. Since you are already comfortable with the Raspberry Pi Pico and LoRa modules (as seen in your recent projects), you can achieve this with a "sleep-and-pulse" architecture that runs for months on a single 18650 cell.

The Scale Strategy: Load Cells

Instead of a wedge-style scale—which suffers from friction issues and repeatability errors—use a Cantilever Load Cell (HX711) integrated into a mounting plate.

  • The Hardware: A single 5kg or 10kg "bar" load cell. You mount your swarm trap on top of a custom base plate where the load cell acts as the fulcrum.
  • Calibration: You calibrate once in software ($Weight = (ADC_Raw - Tare_Offset) / Scale_Factor$). Because the box weight is constant, you aren't measuring absolute weight; you are measuring the delta (empty box weight vs. occupied).
  • Power Efficiency: A Pico in deep sleep consumes $\sim 20\mu A$. By waking it once every 4–6 hours to take a reading, transmit via LoRa, and return to sleep, you can get 6+ months of life on a 3000mAh battery.

Comparative Detection Methods

Thermistor ArrayMediumVery LowLowIdentifying brood rearing (stable 35°C).
Acoustic (MEMS)HighHighHighReal-time swarm monitoring/health.

The "Behavioral" Alternative: Thermal Signatures

If you want to avoid mechanical strain, temperature is your best proxy for activity. A colony must maintain brood nest temperature at 35°C (95°F).

  • The Setup: Place a digital sensor (DS18B20) in the center of the frame area and one outside the hive.
  • The Tell: An empty box tracks ambient temperature (with a slight lag). An occupied box will show a persistent 15–20°C offset from ambient, specifically staying locked at 35°C regardless of nighttime drops.
  • Pros: Requires almost zero power; no moving parts to clog with propolis.

Why Avoid Propolis/Chew-Through Triggers?

As you noted, scavengers are the primary failure point. Ants, wax moths, and mice will chew through thin barriers (wax foundation, paper, or light plastic) just as effectively as bees. To differentiate, you need binary intent:

  1. Weight: Only a swarm has enough consistent mass (a medium swarm is ~3-5 lbs) to trigger a threshold change that persists overnight.
  2. Heat: Scavengers are ectothermic; they won't maintain a consistent 35°C core temperature.

Recommendation: Build a Load Cell Base. Since you already have the 3D printer and design skills, print a base plate that houses a 10kg load cell. It solves the calibration issue (it's fixed in place) and provides the most reliable "swarm arrived" signal without constant maintenance.

turns.prompt_text: What exactly is a load cell base? Could I design some sort of spring using mechanical properties only so that the spring falls below some threshold at some specific weight?
turns.response_html:
What is a Load Cell Base?

A load cell base is a mounting structure designed around an electronic strain-gauge load cell (typically an aluminum "straight bar" or cantilever load cell).

  • The Mechanism: An aluminum bar has four tiny resistors (a Wheatstone bridge) glued to it. When weight is applied to one end, the bar flexes at a microscopic level (fractions of a millimeter), changing its electrical resistance. An amplifier board (like the HX711) converts that resistance shift into a digital weight reading.
  • The Construction: It typically consists of two parallel plates separated by the load cell:
    • Bottom plate: Bolted to the fixed end of the load cell and mounted to your shelf, stand, or tree strap.
    • Top plate: Bolted only to the free/cantilevered end of the load cell and cradling the hive box.
    • Air gap: A small clearance between the two plates ensures that 100% of the box's downward weight passes through the aluminum bar rather than resting on the bottom plate.

Designing a Purely Mechanical Spring Mechanism

You can build a purely passive mechanical scale using spring deflection to trip a visual signal or a simple mechanical switch.

Under Hooke's Law ($F = k \cdot x$), the displacement ($x$) is directly proportional to the applied load:

$$x = \frac{\Delta m \cdot g}{k}$$

Where:

  • $\Delta m$ is the added swarm mass (a typical swarm weighs 1.5 to 2.5 kg / ~3.5 to 5.5 lbs).
  • $g$ is gravitational acceleration ($9.81\text{ m/s}^2$).
  • $k$ is the spring rate ($\text{N/mm}$ or $\text{lbs/in}$).

How to Design the Mechanism

To make a distinct mechanical state change (like a drop-down flag, a lever arm shift, or closing a dry electrical contact):

  1. Preload the Spring for Empty Box Weight: An empty wooden trap with frames weighs around 6–9 kg (13–20 lbs). Use a spring that remains compressed against a hard mechanical stop under empty box weight so light wind or ambient moisture doesn't create false movement.
  2. Set the Trigger Threshold: Choose a spring constant ($k$) such that adding 1.5+ kg (3.3 lbs) overcomes the preload and forces the mechanism past a detent or trip threshold. For example, a spring rate of roughly 1.5 to 2.0 N/mm gives around 8–12 mm of clean vertical travel when a 4-lb swarm arrives.
  3. Trip a Bistable Visual Indicator (Over-Center Latch): Continuous spring deflection can be hard to spot from a distance. Instead, have the moving plate trip an over-center spring latch or a gravity-weighted high-visibility flag. When the box drops ~10 mm, the latch releases and a bright flag pops down or swings out, staying visible even if the box shifts later.

Mechanical Challenges to Account For

  • Wood Moisture Fluctuations: Unpainted or lightly treated wooden hives absorb and release ambient humidity. A heavy rainstorm or humid week can add 0.5 to 1.5 lbs (0.2–0.7 kg) of water weight to an empty wooden box. The trip threshold must be set safely above maximum wet-weather weight gain.
  • Creep and Temperature in Springs:
    • Metal Coil Springs: Steel springs exhibit virtually zero creep and maintain a consistent spring constant across outdoor temperature ranges.
    • 3D-Printed Plastic Springs: Avoid printed PLA or PETG compliant flexures under continuous static load. Plastics undergo polymer creep (permanent deformation under constant stress) and will slowly sag over weeks, causing false triggers.
  • Friction and Binding: Ensure the vertical motion relies on smooth guide pins, a single pivot hinge, or parallel four-bar linkage so rain, dust, and off-center loads don't jam the moving plate.

The entrance turnstile / corkscrew is a classic mechanical concept, but when applied to honeybees, a few severe biological constraints come into play.

Why a Mechanical Turnstile / Corkscrew Fails

  • Microscopic Mass vs. Friction: A single honeybee weighs roughly 0.1 grams (100 milligrams). The kinetic force an individual bee generates while crawling through an entrance is around a few tens of micronewtons—not enough to overcome static friction or turn the inertia of a physical screw or revolving door, even on precision bearings.
  • Bees Avoid Confined Moving Obstacles: Bees rely heavily on antennae and body clearance when entering a cavity. If an obstacle pushes back or pinches, they either abort, become trapped, or perceive it as an invader/blockage.
  • Propolis and "Burr Comb" Seizure: Any mechanical pivot, shaft, or helical gear placed in a bee pathway will be glued immobile with propolis and beeswax within 24 to 48 hours. Bees seal gaps narrower than their "bee space" (roughly 6–9 mm) with propolis.
  • Mass Congestion During a Swarm Arrival: When a 15,000-bee swarm moves in, they do not enter single-file. They create a mass wave—hundreds of bees rushing the entrance every minute while others fan Nasonov pheromones right on the landing board. A physical turnstile would immediately choke the entrance and cause the swarm to reject the box.

Low-Power Optical Alternatives for Entrance Counting

If you want an entrance-based counter without relying on mass/weight:

  • Infrared Break-Beam Gates:
    • Multiple parallel 3D-printed entry tunnels (each sized to standard bee space, ~8 mm wide).
    • An IR emitter/photodiode pair across each tunnel.
    • When a bee walks through, it cuts the beam. Two offset beams per channel can determine direction (inbound vs. outbound).
    • Drawback: Requires keeping the optics clean and draws continuous (or pulsed) current.

Comparing the Core Detection Approaches

MethodMechanismPrimary Failure ModeViability
Mechanical Weight (Spring/Latch)Box deflection under +3–5 lbsRain soak adding wood tare weightHigh (Passive, no power)
Electronic Weight (Load Cell)Micro-strain on cantilever barCreep/drift over months without tareHigh (Definitive delta)
Propolis / Chew-ThroughBiological sealing/chewingScavengers (ants, moths, mice) cause false positivesLow
Mechanical Turnstile/ScrewKinetic rotation from walking beesInsufficient bee mass & propolis jammingNon-viable
Acoustic / TemperatureNasonov roar (~250 Hz) or 35°C coreHigher baseline energy budgetMedium–High

Weight remains the cleanest differentiator because it measures the single physical property that only an entire swarm provides: instant, multi-pound mass addition.

turns.prompt_text: The method we currently use to see if bees have a swarm in there is to see if there is any nectar on there or pollen on their legs. If there's any pollen on their legs then it means they're making
turns.response_html:
...they're making brood.

That is one of the most reliable visual rules of thumb in beekeeping.

Why the "Pollen on the Legs" Rule Works

  • Scouts vs. Settled Foragers: Scout bees and robber bees only look for cavity dimensions, leftover honey, or sugar. They enter and leave light and fast, carrying no pollen.
  • The Biological Trigger: Bees only collect and pack pollen (protein/fats) into their corbiculae ("pollen baskets") when they have young larvae to feed with royal jelly and bee bread.
  • The Swarm Confirmation: A newly arrived swarm spends the first 24–48 hours drawing fresh comb, after which the queen begins laying eggs. As soon as eggs hatch into larvae (day 3–4 post-laying), the field force immediately starts bringing in heavy pollen loads.

If you see steady incoming bees with bright yellow, orange, or white pollen pellets on their hind legs, the box is no longer just being scouted—it is an established, queen-right colony with active brood rearing underway.

The challenge with using food as a "bait" for detection is the "Robber vs. Resident" paradox: anything that attracts a swarm also triggers an immediate feeding frenzy from yellowjackets, ants, wasps, and neighboring honeybee colonies.

If you provide a resource, you aren't just attracting a potential resident; you are opening a scavenger buffet that can actually prevent a swarm from moving in (swarms prefer clean, secure cavities, not "busy" ones filled with fighting insects).

The "Only a Hive Wants It" Resource

There is exactly one substance that acts as an exclusive social pheromone rather than a food source: Bee-Attract (Nasonov pheromone analogs).

While not a consumable in the sense of "fuel," it is the only resource that acts as a social catalyst.

  • The Science: When a scout bee finds a perfect cavity, she releases Nasonov pheromone (citral and geraniol-based) to recruit the rest of the swarm.
  • The Detection Logic: If you place a timed-release Nasonov lure in the trap, you are "hacking" their recruitment signal. However, this attracts scouts—not necessarily residents.

Why Quantity Won't Filter Scavengers

Increasing the volume of resources (e.g., a quart of sugar syrup or a frame of honey) fails as a filter because:

  • The "Tragedy of the Commons": If you offer an unlimited resource, you create a scent trail that draws in every scavenger within a 2-mile radius.
  • Defense Behavior: A real hive defends its resources. Scavengers (robbers) will ignore the trap if it is occupied by a strong, defensive colony. If the trap is empty, the resource will be picked clean by ants and wasps regardless of the volume.

The "Behavioral Gold Standard": Queen Mandibular Pheromone (QMP)

If you want a "resource" that guarantees you have a resident queen (and thus a full hive), look for Queen Mandibular Pheromone.

  • The Reality: This is biologically expensive and volatile. It is why beekeepers use "Swarm Lures" (the synthetic version) to entice them, but it doesn't keep them.
  • The Only True Filter: The only way to filter "scavengers" from a "hive" is to verify the presence of a queen’s brood nest.

The Strategy: Synthetic "Brood" Detection

Instead of adding a resource for them to eat, monitor the byproduct of their residency.

A colony must produce heat ($35^\circ\text{C}$) and exchange gas ($CO_2$) to survive. Scavengers like ants and wax moths cannot produce a sustained $35^\circ\text{C}$ heat signature in a hive-sized volume.

Recommended "Passive" Setup:

  1. Lure: Use a commercial lemongrass oil/Nasonov lure (to get them inside).
  2. Verify: Install a DS18B20 digital thermometer inside the center frame area.
  3. Logic:
    • Ambient Fluctuations: Follows the outdoor air temp ($15^\circ\text{C}$–$30^\circ\text{C}$). Result: Empty.
    • The "Brood Lock": A steady, flat-line temperature of $34^\circ\text{C}$–$36^\circ\text{C}$, regardless of nighttime outdoor drops to $10^\circ\text{C}$. Result: Confirmed Hive.

This creates a "biological lock." The bees must heat the brood, and they cannot do it without being a fully functional, queen-right colony.

turns.prompt_text: So maybe a thermometer is the best way to go. I want to explore all the different methods and types of thermometers. I wonder if there's any like purely mechanical thermometers or things that change with heat I wonder how much of a difference the heat is
turns.response_html:
How Much Heat Does a Colony Actually Make?

The thermal delta between an empty box and an occupied hive is massive, distinct, and biologically locked.

  • Empty Box: Tracks ambient outdoor air within 1–2°C (with a short thermal lag from the wood). If it drops to 10°C (50°F) at night, the interior drops to ~10°C.
  • Scouts / Temporary Clusters: Might temporarily raise the cavity air by 2–5°C while clustered, but the temperature swings wildly with ambient air.
  • Established Swarm / Brood Nest: Honeybees actively thermoregulate their core brood area to a strict 34°C to 36°C (93°F–97°F).

During spring swarm season, nighttime ambient temperatures often drop to 5°C–15°C (40°F–59°F). An occupied hive will maintain a 15°C to 25°C (27°F–45°F) positive delta directly above the cluster relative to ambient outdoor air.

Purely Mechanical & Passive Thermal Indicators

If you want to avoid batteries or microcontrollers entirely, several mechanical principles convert thermal energy directly into visual movement or state changes.

       Bimetallic Strip                 Liquid/Gas Wax Actuator             Thermochromic Pigment
    
     [ Brass ] ───┐                  ┌───[ Piston Rod ]───┐              ┌──────────────────────┐
     [ Invar ] ───┴──► Curls         │   [ Expanding Wax ]│              │ Dark Blue (Cold)     │
                       when heated   └───[ Brass Body ]───┘              │      ▼ (34°C)        │
                                         Linear stroke (~5-10mm)         │ Bright White (Hot)   │
                                                                         └──────────────────────┘

1. Bimetallic Strips & Coils

  • The Physics: Two metals with different coefficients of thermal expansion (e.g., brass and invar) are bonded together. When heated, the brass expands faster than the invar, causing the strip to curl.
  • How to use it: A bimetallic spiral coil (the core of traditional dial thermometers) placed in the upper frame space can rotate a high-contrast external indicator needle or trip a spring-loaded gravity flag when the internal temperature crosses 32°C (90°F).

2. Thermal Wax Actuators (Linear Thermostats)

  • The Physics: A sealed brass cylinder contains a paraffin wax compound engineered to melt and expand at a specific phase-change point. The volumetric expansion pushes a mechanical piston outward with high force (often 10–50+ lbs of linear thrust).
  • How to use it: Greenhouses use these to open vents passively without electricity. A compact wax actuator rated for 30°C–35°C placed inside the hive can physically push a mechanical trip-pin or drop a visual signal tab outside the box.

3. Liquid/Vapor Expansion Actuators (Bulb & Capillary)

  • The Physics: A liquid-filled sensing bulb placed between frames connects via a narrow capillary tube to a mechanical bellows or Bourdon tube outside the box. As internal heat rises, hydraulic pressure expands the bellows.
  • How to use it: Provides reliable mechanical displacement outside the hive without putting the mechanical linkage right in the bee space where bees can propolize it.

4. Thermochromic Dyes & Pigments (Zero Moving Parts)

  • The Physics: Micro-encapsulated leuco dyes change molecular structure at calibrated temperature thresholds, shifting from opaque/dark to completely clear/colored.
  • How to use it: A target painted with 33°C (91°F) thermochromic paint mounted on the top cover or underside of an inspection window shifts color instantly when heated by the cluster beneath it.

Comparison of Temperature Sensing Methods

Bimetallic Coil/LatchDifferential expansionZero (Passive)Low (Exposed moving joints)Medium
Wax Linear ActuatorParaffin phase changeZero (Passive)High (High piston force breaks propolis)High
Capillary BellowsHydraulic fluid expansionZero (Passive)High (Bulb has no moving parts)High
Thermochromic TargetLeuco dye phase shiftZero (Passive)High (No moving parts)Medium (Needs sightline)

The Practical Verdict

If staying purely mechanical, a wax motor / thermal actuator or a remote bulb & capillary bellows is vastly superior to exposed bimetallic strips because moving hinges inside a bee cavity get glued with propolis. The linear expansion force of a wax actuator easily shears through minor wax or propolis accumulation.

If using ultra-low-power electronics, a single DS18B20 stainless steel probe embedded between the center top bars reading against a reference outdoor probe gives a definitive, quantifiable answer with zero moving parts to jam.

...it should not be drawing almost any power at all. If you only wake up once a day or a few times per day, the system will spend 99.99% of its life in deep sleep, easily lasting entire swarm seasons on standard AA batteries or a single lithium cell.

The Power Budget Reality

A microcontroller only consumes real current while taking readings or transmitting. The rest of the time, its internal clocks and peripherals are powered down.

  • Deep Sleep: ~15–25 $\mu\text{A}$ (microamps)
  • Waking & Reading a Probe: ~5–10 mA for 100 milliseconds
  • Transmitting a Burst (e.g., LoRa / 1-bit radio): ~100–120 mA for 150 milliseconds
  • Average Current (Reading 4x/day + Sleep): < 0.025 mA

A pair of standard AA batteries (approx. 2500 mAh capacity) or an 18650 cell (3000 mAh) will yield 3–5+ years of theoretical standby life—meaning battery shelf self-discharge is practically your only limiting factor.

Low-Power Architecture Options

                   [ Ultra-Low-Power Wake Architecture ]

   ┌───────────────────────┐
   │ RTC Timer (TPL5110)   │ ──(Powers ON system every 4-6 hrs)──► [ Microcontroller ]
   │ (Draws ~35 nA)        │                                               │
   └───────────────────────┘                                       Reads Temp & Delta
                                                                           │
   ┌───────────────────────┐                                               ▼
   │ DS18B20 Temp Probes   │ ◄──(Power gated via GPIO pin)───────── [ Decision Engine ]
   └───────────────────────┘                                               │
                                                                           ▼
                                                             [ Transmit / Visual Flag ]

1. Hardware Power-Gating (The TPL5110 Nano-Timer) Instead of relying on microcontroller sleep firmware, you place a TPL5110 nano-timer chip between the battery and your microcontroller board:

  • The entire microcontroller is completely unpowered (0 $\mu\text{A}$) while waiting.
  • The timer draws only 35 nanoamps ($0.000035\text{ mA}$).
  • At your set interval (e.g., every 2 hours), the timer gates power to turn on the board.
  • The board takes a reading, decides if a swarm is present, fires off a signal or logs the data, and asserts a "DONE" pin to tell the timer to cut power entirely.

2. GPIO Power-Gating Sensors Standard digital sensors like a stainless-steel encapsulated DS18B20 digital thermometer draw quiescent current if left connected to $V_{CC}$.

  • Wire the sensor’s $V_{CC}$ pin to a GPIO pin on your microcontroller instead of permanent power.
  • Pull the GPIO HIGH only for the 100ms needed to read the 1-Wire temperature, then pull it LOW before sleeping.

The Minimalist Decision Logic

To avoid false triggers from hot summer afternoons:

  1. Read Two Probes:
    • $T_{\text{internal}}$: Centered between the top bars in the middle frame.
    • $T_{\text{ambient}}$: Mounted on the shaded underside of the hive stand.
  2. Evaluate the "Brood Lock" Condition:
    • If $(T_{\text{internal}} \ge 34^\circ\text{C})$ AND $(T_{\text{internal}} - T_{\text{ambient}} \ge 8^\circ\text{C}\text{ at night})$, flag as OCCUPIED.
    • If both track ambient within $\pm 2^\circ\text{C}$, flag as EMPTY.
  3. Action:
    • Transmit a single 1-bit status byte or trip an external low-power latching indicator.

Do You Need an External Circuit for Power Management?

No, you do not need an external circuit (like a TPL5110 nano-timer), but it depends on which specific board you grab from your bench:

  • Non-Wi-Fi Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040):
    • The RP2040 chip has a built-in hardware Real-Time Clock (RTC) and an internal DORMANT sleep mode that drops the chip itself down to ~0.8 mA.
    • On a bare Pico board, the on-board RT6150 buck-boost regulator still burns about 1.3–1.5 mA continuously in sleep. That will drain a pair of AA batteries or an 18650 in 2–3 months instead of years.
  • ESP32 (Standard DevKit):
    • The ESP32 silicon has a dedicated Ultra-Low-Power (ULP) co-processor and RTC timer that draws only 10–15 $\mu\text{A}$ in deep sleep.
    • The Catch: Typical $4 breadboard dev boards (NodeMCU / ESP32-WROOM kits) include a cheap linear voltage regulator (AMS1117) and a USB-to-UART bridge chip (CP2102/CH340) that stay powered on, pulling 10–25 mA constantly, killing a battery in days.
  • The Verdict:
    • If you use a bare ESP32 / bare Pico or a power-optimized board (like an Adafruit Feather / Seeed Xiao), you can use pure onboard deep sleep with no extra chips.
    • If you are using a standard off-the-shelf development board, a $2 external hardware timer (like the TPL5110) or a single low-quiescent LDO bypass is the easiest way to cut that vampire power to near zero without desoldering onboard LEDs or chips.

Adding Acoustic / Noise Detection Without Killing Battery

Adding a microphone module is a smart complementary check—swarms produce a distinct acoustic roar (200–300 Hz wing-fanning) right when they arrive.

                                                                   │

                                                       [ Log / Set Visual Latch ]
                                                                   │
                                                                   ▼

How to Add Audio on a Micro-Power Budget

  1. Never Stream Raw Audio Continuously: Continuous FFT analysis or audio sampling will chew through hundreds of milliamps.
  2. Duty-Cycle the Microphone:
    • Power the microphone module (like an analog MAX4466 or MAX9814) directly from a microcontroller GPIO pin rather than the permanent 3.3V rail.
    • When the timer wakes the board, pull the GPIO HIGH, take 50–100 rapid ADC samples over ~200 milliseconds to calculate RMS amplitude (or run a quick Goertzel algorithm targeting 250 Hz), and immediately pull the GPIO LOW.
  3. Threshold Logic:
    • An empty box inside has near-zero internal acoustic energy (except for wind/rain on the roof).
    • A fresh swarm creates sustained, high-amplitude white noise and low-frequency resonance that easily clears a digital RMS threshold.

turns.response_html:
You are spot on about catching the initial arrival roar—a swarm's collective fanning frenzy only lasts 30 to 90 minutes while they scent the entrance, so an hourly polling cycle will almost certainly miss that brief event.

Using the microphone only as a secondary confirmation once a thermal anomaly occurs is a solid, energy-conscious strategy.

Energy Efficiency: Temperature vs. Microphone

  • DS18B20 Temperature Probe: Draws ~1 mA for about 100 ms to perform a 12-bit conversion, transferring data via digital 1-Wire. Total energy per read is virtually zero.
  • Analog Microphone (e.g., MAX4466): Draws ~0.5–1 mA, but requires the microcontroller's CPU and ADC to stay awake at full clock speed for several hundred milliseconds to sample enough audio frames to compute an RMS average or frequency baseline.
  • The Verdict: Temperature is far more energy efficient. Polling temperature first and only firing up the audio sampling pipeline if $T_{\text{internal}}$ climbs above ambient avoids unnecessary CPU cycles.

Battery Life Reality: Dev Board vs. TPL5110 Nano-Timer

Swarm season in the Midwest runs from late April through early July—a solid 2.5 to 3 months.

If you take a standard development board off your bench and power it directly from an 18650 cell (~2500–3000 mAh):

  • Standard Dev Board (Native Deep Sleep):
    • The onboard linear regulator and USB-UART chip pull roughly 1.5 mA continuous vampire draw.
    • Battery Life: $\frac{2500\text{ mAh}}{1.5\text{ mA} \times 24\text{ h/day}} \approx \mathbf{69\text{ days (under } 2.5\text{ months)}}$.
    • It will be cutting it extremely close or dying right at the peak of the season.
  • With a TPL5110 Power-Switching Chip (~$2 module):
    • Hardware completely cuts power to the board between reads (draws 35 nanoamps).
    • 4 readings a day burns <0.05 mAh per day.
    • Battery Life: Over 2 to 3 years on a single 18650 cell (limited only by the battery's internal shelf self-discharge).

Adding that little external power-gating board removes all stress about board-level vampire draw, eliminating the need to add bulky parallel batteries or wire up solar panels.

Battery vs. Small Solar

  • Battery + TPL5110: Pure plug-and-play. No weatherproofing concerns for glass panels, no tree canopy shading issues, and no extra charge-controller circuitry. A single 18650 easily outlasts the entire season.
  • Solar Panel Addition: A tiny 5V 1W solar cell with a TP4056 lithium charging board allows a standard dev board to run without an external power cut-off timer. However, swarm traps are usually placed in deep tree shade or facing north/east to avoid baking the cavity, which significantly degrades solar output.
